p: Thank you for the question. There are a couple of steps. So, first and foremost, MOCJ is looking at all of the criminal legal system as a whole. First and foremost it is ensuring that the programs that do not have people going into Rikers are able and ready for the capacity to support people. So, the Project Resets, the ways that we look at those individuals who are– have a persistent pattern that we are consistently engaging with so that they don’t– they break that cycle of coming back in where you would see them going into Rikers, because now they have accumulated cases and they fall into harm and harm, right? So, the trajectory is usually them increasing and what we’re looking to do with our Intensive Case Management program is identifying those individuals sooner, and truncating the arch of them repeating and coming back into the system by connecting them sooner in the process so the services that would then stop them from going into the system in the first place.
What are steps that MOCJ is taking to ensure that the NYPD is providing evidence in a timely way?

That’s a big ask. So, we work with NYPD. We work with the DA’s offices, and we have looked at the ability to provide discovery across the city. One of the areas that we worked on very closely with NYPD and with the DAs is just the ability to make sure that the systems actually spoke to one another, right? Our First Deputy Director was crucial in navigating the– it’s– the acronym is API, and my public affairs guys is going to kill me, because I use the acronym, but it really is the bridge that delivers the information from PD systems to DA systems, and given that there are five of the electeds, as well as Special Narcotics, it was a feat to make sure that that bridge stayed open with the vendor that PD was using so that we could ensure that there was no gap and that there was no elongating of the time. As they told you earlier, each one of them building their own systems has its– has had the issues we see whenever we’re rolling out new technology across, there have been challenges and delays, but they’re actively working on it, and we’ve been actively working with all of them to navigate some of the places where we have to make sure that

the vendors meet the goals for the city, meaning the DAs and NYPD and the defenders alike.

Alright. And final question before I pass it on to colleagues. Question about ATI and reentry services. The Preliminary Budget includes a $1.3 and $3.3 cut to ATI programming and reentry services. Do we think that it is wise to cut these services? I think the answer to that is no. Are we taking steps to make some restorations?
So, we continue to work with OMB to ensure that we have the appropriate level of services for the– for ATI and reentry.
Okay. Have you started those conversations yet, or?
We’re continuing to work with them on it, yes.
Okay. So, I’ll pause here. I’ll pass it on to Council Member Nurse for some questions.

Thank you. Thank you, Chair. Good to see you all. I have questions I promise. Local Law 139 mandates MOCJ ensure that when assessment is required for acceptance to a court-based alternative to incarceration program, a

holistic clinical assessment shall be completed within three or six– three weeks or six weeks for more complicated cases. We know that the legal mandate just took effect in February. So, you know, kind of what are you all– how are things going? Are we hitting those timelines? Is there capacity for it?
It's a little early to provide specifics. However, we– the program is funded. CJI has received the funding for it, and they are currently working to staff up.
And how long do assessments take on average now?
I would have to get that number for you. I know it varies depending on how complicated the case is.
Would it be fair to say longer than six weeks normally?
Without additional resources, yes, it can take longer.
Okay. And who will be providing the assessments just for the record?
So, we’re working through CJI, but it will be– they’re clinical assessments so it would be clinical staff that’d be doing that.

And then for supervised release, which we’ve talked about a bunch, and over the last couple of years we see the Preliminary Budget as cutting it by– cutting funding for it by $4.5 million. Do you know where those cuts are going to be made, to what parts of the program?
So, we’re continuing to work with OMB on looking at the numbers for SRP over the past year and over years past just to see where those numbers lay, and determining the right level for it.
Okay. Do you know if any of those cuts will be made to some of the intensive case management program?
We do not have that information [inaudible].

Yeah, I would just say that is, you know, something we’ve all been advocating for, especially to safely bring down the jail population and obviously reduce violence and get

people out who might not necessarily need to be there, but might need some extra eyes and ears. So, hopefully we can make sure that the case management is sustained and that we’re able to get people out and continue to bring down the jail population. And quickly on Harbor House, there’s over 100 beds and a month-long waiting list. Do you have any plans to grow the number of residential treatment beds for people with dual diagnoses?
That is a clear gap that we have seen in services and it is something we’re continuing to work on to figure out exactly what the gap is and what that looks like long-term.
But no plans? Nothing in this plan for additional beds?
Not currently.
Okay. From what we’re– what we’ve been told, it sounds like there’s space to add 50 beds which would cost about roughly $3 million to kind of outfit the space. Is that your understanding?
We have heard that from partners, yes.
Okay. Okay. And then I saw that you’re adding from your testimony 100 beds– that’s for the transitional emergency housing? Okay.
Yes, it is.
That’s great. I think thats– and do we know where– sorry. What borough will that be, or is that just across the board?
We’re looking at a few different boroughs. We’re looking in Queens and also in Brooklyn and possibly the Bronx.
Okay. And you don’t have the distribution yet, though.
We don’t have the exact distribution.
Okay. One other– [inaudible] I guess people are joining us virtually, but I have one more question. For the Local Law 92–
[inaudible]
Sergeants?
Alright, please let’s mute all the zooms.
[inaudible] but that should close at like six o’clock.
Yeah, that’s what I’m saying. That’s why–
[interposing] Please mute yourself if you’re on Zoom.

Hopefully they’ll make it by six. Local Law 92 from 2023, there was a resource navigator program for women, transgender, intersex, non-binary, and gender non-conforming people. Is this resource navigator program fully operational and fulfilling its mandate?
We do have within our reentry services resource navigation, and then also we have on our website the ability to go in and search for those services, yes.
Okay. And what budget line item is this program included under?
I don’t think we– I think we were able to do it in a budget neutral way.
I’m sorry, can you bring the mic a little bit closer? Sorry, I’m going deaf.
I’ll turn it over to our
I believe the budget item is included under our reentry budget.
Under reentry? Okay. Okay. Those are my questions, Chair. Thank you.

Thank you so much. A few more questions. A question about the Intensive Case Management pilot. This is a pre-trial supervised release program that provides case workers to those that– who check in and also offer services and provide reminders to people of their court dates and other things. Does the Preliminary Budget include funding to expand on this, or is that something that there’s a planned cut on that program?

Chair, currently the funding is maintained for fiscal year ‘26 at $9 million. There is not an out-year funding at the moment, but we continue to work with OMB to assess the program needs and the fiscal needs to continue the program.

Alright. Similar question, but I guess on the issue of District Attorneys, what steps is MOCJ taking to ensure that District Attorneys and defenders have installed technology so they can process, store and share evidence efficiently? And also, the state approved $50 million for this two years ago. Do we have any

information on when this will be installed and finalized?

So, in working with the DAs, we talk to them about needs and where they are with the discovery. The discovery funding that the state provided went directly to the District Attorneys, and so they are– they managed what they spent those funds on in terms of the technology and their infrastructure bills. Given that each office has its own separate infrastructure, it’s our understanding that they’re in different places and that they are diligently working to get a place of having their systems completed, but we understand that the Bronx started sooner with one of the vendors and may be in a better place to be moving through what the technology looks like. Queens had its own internal database system that it was building out. Manhattan also has a good infrastructure system that it was building out. Staten Island was using a product that was on the state level, be it used by other prosecutors across New York State.

And Brooklyn also is looking at building up its infrastructure. So, each one of them is in a different place and we continuously work with them as well as the Corporation Counsel where there may be challenges with contracting to ensure that they are– resources are being appropriately dedicated towards the technology bills and any challenges are addressed.

Alright. And last question for me: Can you talk to us about some of the criminal justice housing related programs that you have. I know you provide transitional housing for those exiting Rikers. Can you talk about those housing programs a little bit?

Sure. It's our emergency and transitional housing program. We work with three providers to implement that program. It’s the Fortune Society, Housing Works, and Housing Plus which is a consortium for women. And we have about 800 beds open now, and we’re planning for about 150– about a 150 more over the next year.

Alright. Thank you so much. Anyone else has any other questions? Alright, so I

think this concludes this part this of the– Actually, Council Member Wong has a–
[interposing] I’ll squeeze in a question. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Chair. I noticed that you offer services for defendants as well as services for victims. Is that right? No? I’m wrong?
Not quite. We do have some services for victims, yes.
So, how do you balance it because they seem to be, you know, conflicting goals here?

Well, most of the contracts for victim services sit with HRA now. However, we believe that the criminal justice system is– the criminal legal system is a continuum, and everybody needs to– we’re looking at public safety. It helps us both to ensure that victims have what they need and then ensure that people are less likely to reenter the system. So, that’s how we sort of balance the concept.

Thank you, Council Member Wong. And I also want to just highlight the fact that we

are– our community courts deal a lot of work with restorative justice. So that means that instead of looking at a punitive model meaning you did something bad, and so now we’re going to punish you, and the person who was harmed doesn’t necessarily get the justice that they’re seeking. So, restorative models allow both the individual that was harmed and the individual that did the harm to work together to think about what healing really looks like. Because healing doesn’t always mean that we have to put somebody in jail. Healing can be what do I need to do to try to bring you back to the place you were before I did this harm to you, and working together, the person who was harmed and the person who did to the harm come to a resolution as to how the two of them walk away from that scenario stronger and better for the interaction and community is stronger at that point as well.
Okay. Thank you for clarifying.

Thank you. Thank you so much again for joining us today. We look forward to

continuing the conversation on the many topics that we have talked about today, and thank you for the work you do.
Thank you.

Alright. Now we’ll be opening the hearing for public testimony. I remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times. The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. This hearing is already being recorded. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record. If you wish to speak at today’s hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you’ll have two minutes to speak on today’s oversight hearing topic, the budgets of the New York City

Police Department, District Attorneys, CCRB, and MOCJ, the Mayor’s Office of Criminal Justice. If you have a written statement or additional testimony you’d like to submit on the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms. You may also email written testimony to testimony@council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of the close of this hearing. Audio and video recordings will not be accepted. For in-person panelists please come to the table once your name has been called. I’ll now call the first panel, in-person panel, who has already joined: Tina Luongo from the Legal Aid Society, Piyali Basak from the Neighborhood Defender Services, Juval Scott from the Bronx Defenders, Stan German from the New York County Defender Services, and Lisa Schreibersdorf from the Brooklyn Defender Services. So, I guess we can start from left to right, or do you want to start from right to left?
We have an order, so we’re going to go– if it’s okay, we’ll go this way.

Sounds good. And we’ll provide Council Members with four minutes of

questions. For this panel, we’ll provide five minutes for the opening statement. Thank you.

Thank you. Good afternoon Council Members and Chair. My name is Stan German. I’m the Executive Director for New York County Defender Services. Today’s March 18th, in the defender community and courts throughout the country, this is known as Gideon’s Day. 63 years ago the Supreme Court issued the ruling in Gideon V. Wainwright that essentially poor people accused of crimes have the right to counsel, and I’m hoping that’s an omen that in this budget year we are going to see the kind of budgets that reflect the value that all our public defender offices and our staff bring to the criminal legal system. The reality is that in terms of a marketplace, New York City is simply not competitive with the rest of the country. When you look at jurisdictions in large cities like Los Angeles, Atlanta, Seattle, Oakland, San Francisco, all of them have starting salaries for public defenders north of $105,000. When you look at federal defenders who are public defenders in the federal system throughout the country, they have a similar starting salary.

If you look at upstate counties in New York State, closer to home, there are seven counties upstate with a lower cost of living where the starting salary is at $100,000 or less. And if you take into account the cost of living adjustments for cities like Minneapolis and Houston, they are also north of $100,000. New York City continues to lag behind. Now, on the issue of affordability, we’ve been talking about this issue long before it became a mayoral hot topic last year. We’ve been coming to this chamber year after year after year talking about affordability, and the struggles that our staff have in making a livable wage in New York City. You have law students who are graduating with six-figure student loan debts, and yet they choose– they choose to not go into the private sector, but serve the public. We have got to do better by our staff. You’ve asked a lot of questions today, Chair, about ATIs, alternatives to incarceration. You asked MOCJ and you asked the DAs. The reality is that work in large part gets done by the social workers in our offices. That takes preparing clients, discharge

planning, finding drug programs, finding a place to sleep, going through the diversion process at the different DAs offices. It's our staff that are navigating all of that space, and all of us collectively, we need more resources for more social workers. We are not going to close Rikers Island unless we have the kind of social services that the clients are going to need so that we can safely reduce the jail population at Rikers Island. Closer to home, I just want to do a comparison, because you know, at the end of the day, a budget is a value statement. It tells New Yorkers what this chamber values. And over the past four years with the prior administration, a clear value statement was set. N YPD salaries went up significantly. A five-year police officer with minimal overtime makes $150,000 per year. A public defender by contrast it would take them 20 years to make $150,000. The retention problem is real. Our staff are forced to choose between do I have a child and incur all the expenses with child care, or do I stay as a public defender? And what we see increasingly is of course they’re

leaving our offices, whether it’s to buy a home or to start a family. When you lose that experience, again, case processing takes a hit. A more senior lawyer can adjudicate a case more quickly than a younger attorney who’s learning the process. All of this we can tie into our mandate to close Rikers Island, and we need budget increases which my colleagues will address specifically in order to make that happen. Thank you.

Good afternoon and thank you very much, Chair Feliz, and thank you, Council Member Wong, for staying. I’m Tina Luongo. I’m the Chief Defender at the Legal Aid Society. I've been practicing as a public defender in this new– in this city since 2002. Let me start where this actually lives, in the real lives of the people we serve and the people who will likely come as the members of the public to testify about their needs. When New Yorkers are in crisis– New Yorkers are in crisis, when someone’s arrested, when a parent is at risk of losing a child or a child is accused of a crime, when a family's rent is due and a court date is missed because of

work, when a person is terrified about what one mistake could mean for their figure, public defenders and our interdisciplinary teams are the people closest to what is needed and they are closest to where the solutions lie. But here's the hard truth. The City cannot keep asking our teams to carry more crisis, more complexity,and more responsibility while failing to sustain the workforce that makes those outcomes possible. So I want to be clear about what we are asking today and why it can no longer wait yet another fiscal year. We need an infusion into our funding streams above about $100 million to fully support and allow us to be able to work with our staff, many of them unionized, many of them in this audience, many of them watching online who do this work every day so that we can do what actually Stan has just said. Because the reality of this situation is if we don’t, we are not just failing them, we are failing the people who are dragged every day into the criminal legal system, the family separation system and the immigration detention system. Because that is who is at the heart of representing clients and representing those families to turn the system around.

In addition to that $100 million, right now it is critically important to fund immigration representation, and there’s a lot talk in a separate hearing that covers that type of funding for our immigration units, but there is a specific unit in our offices that does work pursuant to the constitution under a case Kentucky V. Padilla [sp?] that indicates that as public defenders, as criminal defense lawyers, we must advise our clients who are in the criminal legal system of adverse immigration consequences. And now more than ever it is critical that we build bigger teams because frankly what we’re falling right now is an increase of the harms given the federal actions across the country and specifically in our city. And then my colleagues will talk about the fact that we need real change in our contracting process, because the way in which our monies flow and the monies flow to other nonprofits. It’s very different than how the money flows to the District Attorneys. And that creates lag times and cash flow issues that are real. So, I turn this now to my colleagues to go more into depth, but this is what's at stake. I’m asking

that we treat our public defenders and our staff the way New York treats other essential services as a core infrastructure that is absolutely critical, and if we do not address this, our attrition will continue and all the things we talked about, about moving and case processing will simply not be available, because at the heart of it is the public defender who needs to represent that person in court. Thank you.

Sorry about that. Good afternoon. My name is Juval Scott. I’m the Executive Director of the Bronx Defenders. Unlike my colleagues I don’t have a career practicing in New York. I came from the federal defender system, and so I’ve been the Executive Director for about 19 months. I’ll admit that as I start these comments, I’m a bit, you know, uncertain of where to begin, because I believe that if we were here to have a serious conversation that we would be treated in a similar way as the District Attorneys, and we would have meaningful conversation, and we would have a panel that was dedicated and allocated to us. And the reason why that would happen is because there’s no way that you increase prosecutions.

There’s no way that you can have a serious inquiry about what prosecutors need without critical understanding of what the constitutional counterpart to the prosecutor’s office is, and that’s public defenders. Today is National Public Defender Day, and today I got to watch the prosecutors praise the City Council for increasing salaries for their staff, making it more comfortable for them to do the work that– the other side of the work that my– the people in my office do. But we’re not able to offer that same praise, because year after year as I understand it, before I got here and even since I’ve been here, we continue to ask City Council, the City, to increase funding for the salary and benefits lines for public defenders in New York City. It is true that federal defenders in New York City make a considerable amount more than public defenders in our offices. Public defenders at about 10 years in the federal defender system make about $196,000. That is far more than what the public defenders in our offices make. But if you look at

cities that are comparable to New York, even that is low. The lowest salary for public defenders in comparable California cities is $134,000 a year. That’s to start right out of law school. That is the starting rate, and the reason why that is meaningful is because it allows young people to come in to focus on the work so that they can do critical work on behalf of the people that we represent, the community that we serve so that they can gain the skills and training and assets needed to do work at the highest level, and so they stay in the work, and so that we’re not constantly having to retrain new people year after year and not keeping institutional knowledge so that people who do come in as new attorneys are able to benefit from their colleagues who remain in the offices. That’s what makes a public defender office great. That’s what makes public defense a sustainable pathway, a career pathway, in large and major cities. And so we ask the city– you know, we ask the City Council as we do every year to increase significantly the salaries on behalf of public defenders. It’s the only way to make the work sustainable. It’s the only

way that we can continue to recruit. And we’d note that people who do this privately and are appointed on cases get paid considerably more than our staff. So, you know, paying institutional providers additional money still realized a cost savings for the city. And so we really would ask that you think about what it means for people to dedicate their career to representing the community’s most vulnerable citizens, and to really think about what it means for them to have to weight whether or not they can pay their bills as they do this work and focus on– they should be able to focus on the work. We ask a lot of our employees, and so we’re asking for you to increase the money that we’re able to pay them and the benefits lines, because it’s not keeping pace. Health care benefits are going up across the board. All benefits are going up and we need to be able to meet the moment, because that is our constitutional mandate. Thank you.

Hi, I’m Lisa Schreibersdorf. I’m the Executive Director of Brooklyn Defender Services. We represent people in Brooklyn and Queens. I interview dozens of people

each year who make the commitment to bring their skills, dedication and talent to helping people who get arrested. When people are arrested, they face a wide variety of lifelong consequences such as loss of educational opportunities, loss of employment, eviction from housing, deportation, and many other harms. Each of these is the responsibility of that person’s attorney, their criminal defense attorney. No matter the seriousness of the underlying case, the impact on the people we represent is wide and deep, and the staff that do this work give themselves to the work, including the support that is needed to deal with these issues, along with things that are affecting our clients such as drug and alcohol use, mental illness, physical illness, impairment, disability, trauma, and poverty. Despite their good work, many of my staff do not have sufficient money to pay their own rent, pay their own utilities, and certainly not to keep up with their student loans. My office is scheduled to conduct collective bargaining this year, and the staff is understandably frustrated that year-in and year-out they come to me

as their leader and just want to be paid a wage that corresponds with the other big cities and which can provide them with a living wage. All of them have given up the financial benefits of working at corporate law firms or even other types of legal work that can be a lot more lucrative. And while they do this important work for the individuals we serve as well as honestly for our very democracy, they are devalued over and over by the city, the city that they call home and the city to which they have devoted themselves. It is not surprising that this has a significant impact on the morale of the office. It is not surprising that people lose hope, not only for themselves, but for their clients and for the systems that they are facing every single day. The issue is a crisis beyond the individual employee who well-deserves this raise. It is existential and now is the time to show that it will end. The progress will be made that there is a commitment by this Council to pay the essential workers that we are. To do that, we must focus a little bit on some boring wonky stuff which is always my assignment.

You’ll get used to that. That’s the procurement process. Unlike our counterparts at the DA’s office, we are not government agencies. We are not elected officials. We are not blessed with free rent, good pensions for our staff or the resources of the entire NYPD, the Medical Examiner’s Office, to work on our cases. We are nonprofits with a contract with the City of New York, and due to that, we are bound to procurement rules that include bidding for our work on a regular basis. And often, the financial barriers that also incumber other nonprofits that are providing an entirely different type of service. The next RFP already are overdue. Our process- RFP process and it’s overdue. It may come out this September for the next fiscal year. It may be delayed again. During these in-between years, the City has historically not provided a real avenue to address specific funding shortfalls which makes it really critical to assure that when this comes out, when this RFP comes out, it has to have the proper amount of funding. And in order to give our staff the salaries that reflect their value and that are competitive, we

estimate as you heard earlier, it’s about $100 million just for staff funding. We have thousands of people working for us. That needs to be added to the RFP. We can’t just talk about it. It needs to be funded before that process begins. That also does not include increases in rent, need for more space which we all have, increases in health insurance, and just about every other everyday item that is part of our budget like pens or computers. We are asking that you please fight for that RFP this year so that our boring and burdensome– yes, I wrote that down as I was sitting here all day– our burdensome procurement process is fruitful and results in a meaningful use of our resources and time. Thank you very much.

Good afternoon, Council. My name is Piyali Basak. I’m the Managing Director for the Neighborhood Defender Service in Harlem. I wholeheartedly join my colleagues in this request for increased funding to support our offices, especially so that we can provide increased salaries. I have until about a year ago I was a public defender before I was in this role representing clients, and I can tell you every single one of our colleagues of our

staff who come into this work come into it with a commitment to serve our communities. And I hope the Council honors that commitment. But I want to focus on our request for additional funding to increase Padilla teams. Immigration Law is complex and subject to the abrupt, dramatic shifts sometimes changing the legal consequences of a criminal case over night. There’s a great deal of nuance and understanding. To understand the status of an individual person based on their history, as well as a specific impact of a plea bargain. Given the high court mandate and the necessity to provide accurate, up-to-date, specialized immigration advice, our offices have hired Padilla attorneys, dedicated attorneys providing this advice. Over the past year, increased ICE presences– and I’m sure I don’t need to educate the Council about that– has created a sharp uptick in the need for our Padilla attorneys. Our staff had to devote significant time and resources to tracking daily policy changes, court rulings, enforcement practices while also trying to provide clear guidance to our teams.

Our non-citizen clients, they’re terrified. Even those with lawful status face a possibility that even a minor criminal offense can lead to detention and separation and permanent exile from the United States. Our clients require more direct contact and support, and we try to do so by offering that, by providing the social support as well as connection to other resources. We’re constantly monitoring the Department of Correction’s actions, and for clients who have state, we’re providing court and guidance when it’s needed. We help connect them to attorneys, and we are also constantly providing access to our clients, to immigration teams who are receiving nonstop calls about check-ins with immigration authorities and questions about ICE presence at schools and homes, and other concerns they might have. And so we are asking the Council for additional funding and $10 million to our overall budget so that MOCJ can distribute these funds to our offices. This sustained and expanded funding for this unit will allow us to continue providing this essential

guidance, responding to the increasing complexity of these immigration cases. Thank you.

Alright. Thank you all for being here. Thank you for your testimony and also for all the work you do for our city and the people of this city, especially those that are under some of their most vulnerable positions. So, I have a few questions about salary, retention, and then funding. Salary– I used to be a tenant attorney for Bronx Legal Services. The same issues that all of you mentioned I saw at basically the office training new lawyers, law school graduates generally, spending lots of resources training them, and then two years later they lose them. So they have to start all over which, you know, obviously not a good system. So, on that issue, what would be– what do you think should be, I guess, the proper starting salary, and also how much funding would it require to get there. I think I heard $100 million, but I just want to make sure that I’m putting that on the right issue.

And I think Stan mentioned it, that, look, a starting salary for somebody up in Schenectady, New York, was a $102,000. So, if you

look at that as a benchmark. Certainly we believe that we have to at a minimum look at our upstate counties and come to– but that– think about that, because you have to factor in cost of living. But at some point, we have to be realistic that $100,000 starting salary is something that we should start to think about and implement. And then realize that there have to be consistent cost of living increases to keep pace with inflation. What my colleague Lisa testified to is when our contracts are held flat year after year during our comp– sixth year and now upwards of eight years of contract. Because we are nonprofits, if our rent goes up, if our health care goes up, the only– we don’t get extra money and so then you have to start then thinking about how am I making a choice as a manager to have to both increase the salary which is what we need, or not then pay the increase in the rent on the space we need. My colleagues in the District Attorney offices do not have that problem, do not have that problem. And so it’s not only about the starting salary, but then it is about experience. We talked a lot about case processing and that really is about for us, not about

cases, but about people, our clients. And so if you have an attorney who is taking on a serious case where someone is incarcerated, and they leave because they can’t afford it any longer. That client has to get transferred to another lawyer, and that lawyer cannot pick up the case, that case, and meet that client and run off to trial. They now need to take the time to relearn everything and build a relationship. And I have had a situation where clients are in– at Rikers on serious chargers, and in the span of that case, two attorneys have left the office. Now, it’s not their fault. They were just that breaking point. So, besides starting salary, we must look at the experience and what it means to keep experienced attorneys in our office.

I just want to put some actual like hard numbers. You heard $100 million for salaries– would get us 200,000 starting point, maybe a little more which is what we really need, but also help us get raises across the years and including also our supervisors and other people to train all the new people, but I think there probably needs to be about another $50 million, I’m guessing.

And again, none of us really know, but if you’re asking for a specific number, we– when this RFP comes out, it probably needs to have exactly what it, you know, what it’s currently funded at, which is hard for any of us to glean out of the budget. Let’s be real about it. Plus $150 million, and that should be part of the procurement process where each of us can then go to MOCJ and explain exactly how we plan to use the money that, you know, we need to do this, and I feel like if that amount got into our, you know, into the flow, it could make a really big difference.

And I would just tag onto that. I’d be remiss if I didn’t just note that the $100,000 figure that they’re tossing out is the floor, not the ceiling. That’s still too low. I just want to make sure that I’m crystal clear there, and also when we’re making the comparison to prosecutors salary city, attorney salaries, keep in mind that what we– you know, our– the pension that they get, we don’t get. So it’s still not parity. Even if the salaries were the exact same or even a little bit more, they’re still not parity. The benefits that you get in working for the city are distinctly different, and

so I just want to be clear. We’re here asking for a lot of money. We’re going to keep asking for money until it's fair.

Would all of you mind sharing the– I guess the starting salary for, I guess, a lawyer at your office? What’s the general starting salary or ballpark? I know for legal services it was like $70-80,000 for those that passed–
[interposing] Yeah, right now this year we’re at $88,000.
A law graduate waiting to be admitted starts at $84,000.
I think my office is right at $90, because we actually gave people raises last year, and you know, and for -what other things like space in order to do that.
We’re also at $84,000 and also we'll be bargaining this year.

Okay. Has the– I guess the retention issue or lack of funding issue, has that led to inability to properly handle cases, including giving them the time and attention that they deserve, including on criminal cases?

Obviously, people have their– defendants have the right to– constitutional right to a lawyer. So what are some of the effects that this has had on that?

I mean, to be clear, no client has shouldered the burden of our burnout. The folks who shouldered the burden are the attorneys and the social workers who remain in the offices who then have to step up and get that work done. And so, Tina just alluded to it. You have an attorney who’s at five years with 70 cases. That person leaves, right, those cases have to be reassigned. They’re assigned in some cases to supervisors, other attorneys, and then their caseloads just went up. So the work is absolutely being done in all our offices. It’s being done at an extremely high level, but the cost is the increasing burnout of our staff, and you just alluded to it. Then we get younger. We have to train all over again, and we’re just– it’s like bailing water, you know, out of a sinking ship. We’re just always struggling to get above board. But client representation and the work always gets done.

Just to add to that, I think what we’re seeing is, again, attorneys leaving about years five, six, seven out, who are starting families who cannot afford the public defender salary to support their families. It’s not just, you know, cases being transferred. It’s a mentorship that gets offered, and it’s so critical as part of the training. It’s sometimes supervisors themselves which that is so hard to replace. We have to train to become a supervisor, but they cannot stay on even with the salary bumps that they get which is, you know, frankly not substantial. We need– we would like to do better. So, it is– that is a huge loss for our offices to have experience and sharing that experience among the staff, because that’s where people learn from.

I would quickly add along to that, one of the trends that you see in public defense at about that mark is that you start to lose a lot of the attorneys of color. So, Black attorneys, Black male attorneys in particular as they want to start families, but other attorneys of color really can’t afford to stay in

public defense, and so it becomes an equity issue. It creates– it really creates a situation where you have no pipeline of Black and Brown people to become supervisors and mentors in offices to ascend to leadership to be able to take on the mantle. And so when you have new, young attorneys of color, people of color come into the office and there’s no leadership that looks like them, they don’t have– you know, you don’t see yourself, right, in the leadership, and so you don’t really see that pathway. You don’t see the longevity in the field, and what that means in the Bronx especially where the bulk of our clients are, you know, Black and Brown, it means that our– the people that we serve don’t see people who look like them representing them. And so it becomes an information gap of sorts. There are things culturally that get lost because, you know, the attorneys don’t necessarily relate to the people that we serve, and then also those conversations are missing in an office. And so, I just want to highlight that equity issue as well, because it’s important. I think it’s something that gets overlooked a lot.

Okay. Has the staffing and retention issue created issues related to case-related delays? For example, lawyers not having enough time. They have to adjourn, so a criminal case gets adjourned, delayed and then adjourned again and delayed?

Yeah, it’s very similar to what we spoke about. One, you have to now assume a colleague who left caseload. You now have that burden. And what happens? As much as you try not to, you have to now triage. You also– it has the effect on the person who is now– who’s the client. They built a relationship with somebody in a situation may I say, where trust is not given often because there should be mistrust because this person is accused and being prosecuted. And we are paid, right, by the same government that is prosecuting them. So building trust is something that our staff has to work very hard to do. And now you are held at Rikers and you get a visit and it’s a different attorney than you know and now trust, and now it starts all over again.

So you have actual what we call case processing issues, but more importantly, you have real value issues there that we have to address in New York City. And I want to say just one more thing about sort of what the effect of attrition is. So everybody might say, like, okay, well you lose a lawyer at step five who is a fully-certified attorney, just put a posting up and fill the role. It’s not going to happen. Here’s why. First of all, it’s like what I call rearranging the chairs on the Titanic. Because if I put a posting up, guess who’s offices they might be coming from, my colleagues, who then put a posting up, and guess what happens? They come from my office. Because the reality is we’re not getting anybody who is an experienced criminal defense attorney coming out of the private sector to join our offices. Why? Because the city and the state raised the assigned counsel hourly rate to $156 an hour. And so, in fact, I have lost people to the panel. I just received a resignation yesterday of a lawyer that started with me in 2002, has worked her entire career in the Bronx office, my Bronx office, who’s leaving to become a member of the Bronx Assigned

Counsel, what we call 18B panel, because she has to make more money for her family. That– I’m going to post for that job. I am not– I promise you, I’m not going to find somebody to apply, and that is the reality of attrition.

I totally agree with all of that, and also add that if you do get people from other jurisdictions, there’s also a lot of training that has to go into that. It’s not as straightforward as somebody that already knows New York and New York City procedures and policies. But I did want to say that, you know, we heard from– you asked a lot of questions today about ATIs and we heard from DAs a lot about, you know, how cases are resolved and all the things that all of us in the criminal legal system are trying to do. And I want to just say that 90-something percent of our cases are resolved through plea bargaining, and most of the work that’s done on plea bargaining is done on our side of things. It is unusual for a DA just to pick up the phone and call you and say would you take this or that. Usually we are the ones to call and say hey, you know, can we take a look at this case together? I

have some information for you. I have something of value. My client expressed to me, you know, that he is using drugs and he’d like to stop, and so can we work it out? And when you have a large caseload, it becomes very, very difficult to find the time to find those little issues or bigger issues and then make that phone call or, you know, email the DA and work it out. And if you want to know what the case processing problem is, that’s where it is. It’s probably not ultimately on, you know, whether you review the discovery or you’re ready for trial if you move to trial. It is almost definitely in the delay before you really have the chance to sit down and really think about what can really work and who can I call to try to make that work. And you heard– you know, I’m a Brooklyn practitioner. Our Brooklyn office, our DAs office has for really generations been doing a lot of work around drug treatment, mental health treatment. We can get those deals, but we have to have doctors looking at our clients. We need social workers involved, and the bigger the case load, the harder it is to do these really nuanced pieces that

ultimately resolve cases, and when they get resolved it quickens up the system a little bit and makes room for, you know, trials and for people to maybe get out of Rikers Island and reduce that population as well. So, I think that’s a piece that really needs to be thought about.

Okay. And I think my final question– last year, the Mayor’s Office of Criminal Justice, their budget included a baseline increase of $20.4 million for public defenders. Has the offices seen these funds? And also, if yes, what are areas that this funding went towards?

So, I’m assuming that was part of the new needs ask we had put in request for what our new needs would be for fiscal year ‘26. I know in our case, some of the positions that were filled is– was a diversion attorney. So, again, this ATI theme. Once a case is resolved by plea and the person is placed in diversion court, that really is almost the beginning of the case, because it could take anywhere from 12 to 18 to 24 months to actually get that person into a program and then graduated from the program.

So, we set up a scenario where once the plea is taken, the case would actually be transferred to an attorney or a group of attorneys that’s dedicated just to working with diversion clients in the diversion court. We also put some of that money toward our homicide team. Our homicide funding had remained flat for seven years, and so we made an additional hire there as well.

Some of that went to technology. It was alluded to earlier today about discovery and sort of, you know, discovery management systems. I also think that might have included monies through an RFP process and for new needs in the appeals process, in the appeals practice which are separate organizations with the exception of Legal Aid. We have an appellate office, but there are separate appellate provider nonprofits throughout this city. And so I think that might include some of that additional money there.
Similar types of things.
Okay.

I would just say what we weren’t able to do is just take that money and just give

raises to our staff. So, we had more staff at the same kind of bad pay.

Okay. And final question. What are some of the most effective ATI programs that you usually work with? ATI and also reentry, pre-incarceration? What are some of the programs that most stand out on the issue of violence, and especially gun violence?

So, Council Member Nurse talked about Harbor House. Harbor House is a great program. They’ve got the capacity for 50 new beds. We absolutely need to make that happen. I think she said it was only $3 million. They’re one of the few, if not the only inpatient program that takes folks with SMIs, serious mental illness. So, Harbor House is definitely one that stands out for me.

I think you're likely going to hear from many, many organizations that are sitting here waiting to testify that are incredible, incredible providers of service, but you did talk about– you did talk about those that do violence prevention, and I can’t not talk about, and I’m sure she’s going to talk about, because I see Erica Ford [sp?] in the

audience. Our crisis management providers at the grassroots levels. We have had a longstanding relationship as part of the Cure Violence Crisis Management system since it was started when it was Council Member Jumaane Williams and not Public Advocate Jumaane Williams. When you think about proactive approaches to violence, particularly working with young people, and the way in which our offices and our teams work with those community organizations, that is the answer to not– not rolling back Raise the Age and not looking at state law change and reforms. It is about providing the services on the ground by those who know what it means to be proactive and what the community needs. And so our ATIs, all of them– all these programs that should have– again, will come here and ask for money, and they should be funded fully, because we cannot do what we do without them to sustain folks in community, because the real answer is proactively funding things before somebody gets into a criminal legal system is also part of what we should all be working toward.

I just want to also add without getting into individual programming, because

so many of them are so wonderful. The most– the more diverse the programming is, the more successful it will be, because one of the best indicators of success is if somebody gets into a program that’s culturally appropriate, speaks their language, and meets their actual needs. So, that’s why we have so many, and it’s really hard to say. For the person that needs– for a young person that needs services, a program that provides services to young people is going to be better, you know, for somebody who’s older might need a different kind of programming, somebody who has a mental illness or, you know, so to the extent that we can really think very critically about the more diversity of programming that we have– one size does not fit all at all, and I think that you heard that from the DA’s offices that they try to use different programs. Having said that, people that are specific– organizations that are specifically equipped to work with people who have been incarcerated or have faced incarceration either before they ever go to jail, while they’re in jail, or after jail are in my opinion the ones that we should focus the most on, because a population of people that have experienced

a kind of a trauma, a kind of experience and something that’s going to impact them for a long time time, and the knowledge of that and the ability to work through that is really critical.

Alright. Sounds good. So, I don’t have any more questions. Does anybody have questions? Alright, thank you so much for joining us today and for all the information. I look forward to working together with all of you on all the issues.
Thank you.

Alright, so next we’re going to hear from some of the union representatives: Jane Fox from UAW 2325, Donald Nesbit from DC37, Tabitha Sheppard, DC37, Olivia Duong, DC37. Thank you for joining us. Going to provide two minutes for every person testifying. You may begin whenever you’re ready.

Hi, good afternoon. Thank you for the opportunity to speak. My name is Jane Fox and I’m the Chair of the Legal Aid Society Attorney’s Chapter at the Association of Legal Advocates and Attorneys, and we are UAW Local 2325. We represent over 3,700 active and retired legal services workers at over 30 nonprofit organizations in New York City and beyond.

We are attorneys, paralegals, social workers, investigators, and support staff. And our union members keep clients in their communities and outside of jails, keep families together, keep clients housed, and make sure New Yorkers have access to vital social services. We are the workers who guarantee community safety. And while our members are an essential labor force, decades of underfunding have led to untenable working conditions, and this underfunding has persisted despite our members providing constitutionally-mandated legal representation. We have an attrition crisis and a workload crisis, and this Council needs to start paying attention to this crisis, because when we leave, New Yorkers who depend on us for justice suffer. Our message is simple. Our fight for increased funding has one guiding light. Working class New Yorkers deserve the same level of representation as rich New Yorkers. But year after year, this city and this council has found money to keep police officers and District Attorneys in their jobs, guarantee them a pension while at the same time our union members have been pushed out, told they are not worthy of an

affordable wage or a dignified retirement, because of the people we represent every day. But you can support us and our clients, your very own constituents, with your budget choices. You can support labor by ensuring there is enough money flowing so that when we get to the bargaining table with our employers, we can settle fair contracts. And this year, over 2,000 of our members will be bargaining including all of the criminal trials providers, the Legal Aid Attorneys Chapter, Bronx Defenders, Brooklyn Defender Services, and Neighborhood Defenders. And if I may just wrap up. In fiscal year 2027 we’re asking the Council to fully fund legal services so our employers can meet our core bargaining demands on compensation and retirement, and our costing estimates that the city will need to increase funding by a minimum of $80 million across the legal services sector for our members. As you heard from our employers, they estimate $100 million, because their ask includes non-union staff. We are not siloed to just criminal trials work. This funding will also cover our members providing families, civil, and immigration

representation along other city contracts. And just to note, this $80 million is in addition to what has already been guaranteed in the Preliminary Budget. Our members are not immune from the affordability crisis, austerity budgets and legal services hurt our union and they hurt New Yorkers, and settling fair contracts will provide stability and ensure working class New Yorkers get the absolute best legal representation, because they deserve nothing less. Thank you.

Good afternoon, Chairman Feliz and distinguished members of the Council. It’s an honor to be here. My name is Donald Nesbit, Executive Vice President for Local 372 representing our school crossing guards, level one’s and level two’s within the New York City Department under the leadership of President Sean Francois [sp?]. We– Local 372 has long testified for the hiring of more school crossing guards. It’s vital in order to keep our children safe from dangers of reckless drivers and to ensure the school crossing guard members themselves are not stretched thin and are safe themselves.

Student pedestrians also face major safety traffic hazards every day while going to and from school. This risk is not only a health, safety, and their lives, they perform– they put everything on the line, our school crossing guards. We get calls from community advocates, from CECs and from school principals who often send parent coordinators, school aides, and others in the school building to make sure there’s safety, because there is no school crossing guard on their corner. In 2023, Mayor Adams authorized the elimination of 500 open school crossing guard positions. We are respectfully requesting that those are– that those lines are reinstated and maintained. There has been a number of casualties since then. Christina Napawosk [sp?] school crossing guard was tragically killed on Woodhaven and Atlantic Avenue. October 20th, 2023, eight-year-old student five blocks away from his school in Queens, tragically killed. An 11-year-old girl in Brooklyn tragically killed. No school crossing guard. By eliminating those positions we send a message to the public that our children are not as important. Throughout the couple of years there has been coverage of violence

against transit workers also. The Governor implement– and the Council implemented different measures to protect safety for these transit workers, but what’s not heard is the risk that school crossing guards while protecting our children incur while trying to stop cars who are speeding and those who are reckless drivers. We want to push for more school crossing guards. On snow days and days where schools are closed, these same individuals are not paid. I mean, so this leads to where they have to determine if there's a natural disaster or something happens, determine whether they can pay their bills that pay period, our school crossing guards. And so we respectfully request that they be treated similar to DOE support staff, even though they work for the Police Department, they work closely with our schools. And we just thank you for the opportunity to testify before the Council.

Hello, good afternoon, Chair Feliz and Council Member Phil Wong. My name is Olivia Duong. I am President of Local 3778 of District Council 37, representing 300 civilian NYPD

professional titles such as criminalists, data research scientists, architects. I’m here to highlight the urgent need for a new facility for our hardworking forensic scientists or criminalists at the NYPD police laboratory. We work in the NYPD Detective Bureau and provide– analyze different types of evidence involved in alleged crimes such as drugs, latent finger prints, gunshot residue, firearms using accredited scientific methods. We provide investigative information to detectives and the District Attorneys across all five boroughs as well as the federal government. Criminalists also testify in court as expert witnesses. Our testimony educates juries to make informed and fair verdicts. The need for an updated forensic laboratory building is very long overdue. Currently, there are just under 400 employees working in forensic chemistry, firearms analysis, and crime scene units out of a five-story building in Queens built in 1930. Originally a department store refitted as a college university, and currently a chemical laboratory, firing range, and office building all in one. The

current facility is outdated and in a constant state of repair and disrepair. Millions of dollars have been put in and continue to be put in just to ensure that the roof does not leak. Our operations have long outgrown the space provided for our testing needs. We are working out of laboratory spaces where there are 16 to 20 people in a room, constant flow of traffic around our fume hoods. Let me wrap up– where hazardous chemicals are being used. Our workers deserve a state-of-the-art facility with ventilated spaces where we can handle bulk powder evidence of unknown origin and safe spaces to test life firearms. I ask the committee to ensure that this is put into the NYPD capital budget on behalf of the civil servants who are rarely seen or heard of, but make a profound impact to public safety in New York City. In spite of the many facility challenges we face, my colleagues have strived to maintain the highest quality and integrity of their forensic work for the citizens of New York City every day. Chair Feliz, I'll submit a more detailed version of my testimony for the record, and thank you for the opportunity to speak today.

Thank you. Thank you so much for your testimony. Next, we’ll call our organizations with the great work on the issue of violence prevention, Reverend Wendy from the Urban Youth Alliance Inc., Megan French-Marcelin from the New York ATI Coalition, Nadia from CASES, Lily Shapiro from ATI Reentry Coalition, Madeline Hopper from the Women’s Prison Association, Isabel Greenberg, Center for Employment Opportunities. Alright.

Thank you, Chairman Feliz and members of the Committee. My name is Megan French-Marcelin. Today, I testify on behalf of the New York City Alternatives to Incarceration and Reentry Coalition. We are a network of 12 service organizations with decades of experience in providing community-based supports to justice-involved New Yorkers. In fiscal year ‘25, our organization served more than 68,000 New York City residents. I sit before you as providers face $4.6 million in cuts to ATI and reentry services in the Preliminary Budget. This is despite what we know about the role these programs play in shoring up public safety.

For many decades, the vast majority of the state’s incarcerated population hailed from just seven neighborhoods in New York City. That trend has shifted with the enrichment of services that our coalition provides. Studies routinely show that where neighborhoods invest in community-based providers, crime, even serious crime drops dramatically. Research also demonstrates that these programs are more successful than incarceration at improving public safety outcomes, decreasing the chance of future convictions, reducing homelessness and psychiatric hospitalizations, and inspiring civic engagement. Their price point is also much lower. The cost of incarcerating one person on Rikers for one year is over $500,000. For that, approximately 50 New Yorkers could be taken through life-transforming programming. This year, we are asking the administration for the restoration and expansion of funding for ATIs and reentry services, a $24.6 million increase from what is proposed in the Preliminary Budget.

From the City Council, we are requesting an additional $2.4 million increase in the Alternatives to Incarceration Discretionary Fund across our 12 organizations. These funds have been critical for our programs and the communities we serve. Thank you.
Thank you.

Good afternoon, Chair Feliz and members of the Committee. My name is Lily Shapiro, and I’m Policy Counsel for the Fortune Society’s David Rothenberg Center for Public Policy. Thank you for the opportunity to testify about our work and about how ATI and reentry programs are essential in promoting public safety and assistance while empowering people to successfully rebuild their lives. In fiscal year 25, Fortune served more than 18,000 New Yorkers through our broad array of programs including employment services, mental health and substance use treatment, and our continuum of housing, and this includes the more than 1,000 people we serve through our ATI programs. Every day, we see how comprehensive community-based programming and interventions can

change lives, break cycles of involvement in the justice system and create safer communities for all of us, which is why we are proud to be a member of the New York City ATI Reentry Coalition, and therefore we’re requesting that the administration restore and expand funding for ATI and reentry services an increase of $24.6 million above what is proposed in the Preliminary Budget, and we also request an increase of $2.4 million in the Council’s Alternatives to Incarceration and Reentry Programs initiative. We are very grateful that the Council stood with us in preventing our funding from being cut in fiscal year ‘26 and urge the Council to stand with us again not just to prevent cuts, but to ensure increases to support expansion of this collective work. In fiscal year ‘25, 83 percent of our participants successfully completed their ATI program, and 92 percent of participants, many of whom are youth and young adults, successfully completed gun diversion programming. And the successes behind these statistics are best illustrated by the remarkable participants whose stories are detailed in my written testimony.

I also want to highlight our court navigator program in partnership with the Manhattan DA’s office which in fiscal year ‘25 allowed us to provide immediate resources voluntarily to over 1,000 people, complete full intakes with over 1,100 people and even house 33 people. These are people walking out of arraignments with no court obligations at that time, and this is all on a voluntary basis. This is a program that should be scaled up. Thank you so much for the opportunity to testify today about these critical services and supports.

I’m not going to speak that fast, but I am going to try. I was like, how is she doing this? Sorry. Okay. Thank you, Chairman Feliz and the members of the Committee. It’s nice to see you. My name is Reverend Wendy Calderone-Payne and I’m the Executive Director of Urban Youth Alliance. Many of you guys know us as Bronx Connect and Release the Grip [sic] and we are actually in your neighborhood, Chairman Feliz. We’re a longstanding member of the ATI Coalition. Our organization provides alternatives to young

people, adults, families who are system-impacted and many are court-involved and under court supervision, and we are actually indigenous. We came up from the community, and for over a decade, close to two decades– for over a decade we were the only people placing services in the Bronx. Our position is simple, public safety and public health are not competing goals. Over two decades of experience have shown us that the fastest way to reduce recidivism is to help young people stabilize their lives and connect them to community. New York City’s thriving ATI justice movement has demonstrated that creating safer neighborhoods requires high-touch relationships alongside concrete opportunities such as workforce training, stipends, job placements, partnerships, and credible messengers who can speak to our young people from where they have actually walked. Our Bronx Connect program uses things like restorative justice and cognitive behavioral approaches to bridge these significant gaps. We have a tremendous success rate. 97 percent of our graduates in our high felony program go three years

without a felony reconviction, and that is a national high average. We know that these programs are effective. We know that all of our programs are effective which is why we created the landscape of youth services for young people with juvenile and criminal legal system involvement. I really hope that you guys read it because it’s rich with information. We are asking for expanded family court alternatives to detention programs, $30 million. Development and promotion of new programs that connect youth to year-round employment, that’s the Asvep [sp?] program for the Cure Violence, $3.1 million, and we’d love you to double the court-involved youth mental health program because that has been an excellent program. Thank you so much for allowing me to testify.

Good afternoon, Chair Feliz. I’m Nadia Chait, I’m the Senior Director of Policy and Advocacy at CASES. We serve over 12,000 New Yorkers annually, including over 2,000 who’ve avoided incarceration through participation in our ATI programs. And I second my colleague’s requests for

$24.6 million in city funding and an additional $2.4 million in the Council’s ATI funds. Several of our ATIs focus on serving folks with serious mental illness and helping them get the care that they need in the community instead of being incarcerated. In our Nathaniel Act program which is our most intensive service, we find that among our clients, none are reconvicted of a violent felony, and less than five percent are reconvicted of any felony. The program decreases homelessness by 70 percent and cuts psychiatric hospitalizations in half which is a remarkable success for folks who in many cases have been dealing with persistent mental illness for decades without having access to the treatment that they need and the support that they need. At the other end of the spectrum is New Start which is a much less intensive ATI that’s designed to be a rapid intervention for people with low-level offenses. I want to share what one of our clients recently shared with us. He said, I am so surprised at myself. Today, I feel like staying clean. In fact, I want to help others with sobriety. Someone helped me

stay clean, and now I want to give that to others in my community. And that’s really the success of our programs in action is people seeing not only the benefit of having their own lives, but wanting to share that with others. We’re also one of the intensive case management pilot sites, and we urge the Council to maintain full funding for the pilot which is serving several hundred folks annually. And I’ll very quickly highlight one client’s case, an individual who came into the program a few years after her husband was unfortunately tragically murdered in front of her which led her to developmental health challenges, to abuse alcohol, and to become street homeless. Since her connection into ICM and particularly with a peer specialist, she has actually now been approved for an intensive mobile treatment team to receive the mental health services that they need. She has connected to stable housing and she’s receiving substance use treatment. Thank you.

Good afternoon. My name is Madeline Hopper and I’m representing the Women’s Prison Association. Thank you, Chair Feliz, for the opportunity to testify. For 181 years, the Women’s

Prison Association has been a force for change, supporting system-impacted women across every borough and at every stage of their engagement with the justice system. Decades of direct service show us this. Real public safety doesn’t come from locking women up. It comes from stable housing, access to effective social services and deep community connections. For many women, system involvement is not the result of a single incident, but of systemic failures, poverty, housing instability, and trauma. Women enter the criminal legal system with complex unmet needs and incarceration exacerbates these challenges. When women return home from incarceration, they encounter a reentry system that is underfunded and underequipped. Last year, 60 percent of the women we served in our reentry program lacked stable housing upon intake. WPA envisions a different path. By meeting women and gender-expansive people where they are, we address root causes through individualized diversion and reentry programs that combine wrap-around case management, safe and stable housing, and trauma-informed, gender-responsive clinical care.

These supports stabilize women, strengthen families, and enhance public safety. Programs like our work. They reduce recidivism and cost a fraction of what the city spends on the ineffective and inhumane approach represented by Rikers Island. This year, we are asking the administration for the restoration and expansion of funding for ATI and reentry services at MOCJ, a $24.6 million increase from what is proposed. From the Council, the ATI and Reentry Coalition is requesting an additional $2.4 million increase in the ATI and Reentry program initiatives across our 12 organizations. In addition, WPA seeks additional discretionary funding to expand key mental health and housing services and meet the need for an innovative mother-centered diversion pilot on Rikers Island. In closing, system-impacted women’s needs are unique and our responses must be too. When we support them, families thrive and communities are safer. Thank you.

Can you hear me? Okay. Good afternoon, Chair Feliz and committee members. My name is Isabel Greenberg and I’m a Policy and

Business Development Associate with the Center for Employment Opportunities, CEO, and I want to thank the committee for holding this hearing today. I’m submitting this testimony on behalf of the CEO and the ATI Coalition to highlight the critical length between reentry resources and long-term public safety of our city. CEO’s mission is to provide immediate, effective, and comprehensive employment services to individuals recently returning home from incarceration. As the largest provider of reentry employment services in New York, we serve individuals on probation and parole supervision with the highest risk of recidivism, and have served over 47,000 New Yorkers since 1996. Independent evaluations show that for every one dollar of public investment into our program, $3.30 is returned, and our program reduces recidivism by 22 percent and increases employment rates by 52 percent. Justice-involved individuals are at highest risk immediately following release. By providing immediate transitional employment, CEO stabilizes individuals during this critical time. CEO partners with 10 City Council Members to provide

cleanup and beautification services to their districts. Individuals returning to the five boroughs have the opportunity to find immediate employment and reinvest in the communities they call home. CEO applied for FY ‘27 City Council discretionary and supplemental funding to support our reentry employment model, transitional work group program, and expand our barrier removal and supportive services. While our primary focus is employment, we recognize that public safety is built on a foundation of stability. CEO’s mental health and housing assistance referrals such as for my colleagues act as a safety net that prevents lapses in stability that often lead to re-arrest. We work closely with the Department of Probation as a key referral partners and our contract with DOP funds transitional work crews throughout the city. CEO is also a part of this ATI Reentry Coalition, and with additional financial backing we can scale these community-based programs and provide essential support to New Yorkers returning home from incarceration and achieve a safer New York City. So, thank you so much.

Good evening, Chair Feliz and members of the Public Safety Committee. My name is Asa Meta and I’m testifying on behalf of Common Justice, a New York City organization that operates one of the nation’s first alternatives to incarceration programs for serious violent felonies. For too long, our primary response to violence has been incarceration even though we know that incarceration alone does

little to address the root causes of harm or to support the people and the communities affected by it. True public safety requires approaches that center accountability, survivor healing, and long-term stability. Common Justice works in Brooklyn, the Bronx, and Manhattan with people facing significant prison sentences for violent crimes, as well as the survivors of those crimes. With the consent of the person harmed, these cases are diverted into a Restorative Justice process that centers survivor needs while requiring the responsible party to take meaningful accountability. Participants complete an intensive 12 to 15 month program that includes violence intervention, restorative justice dialogue, education, and employment support and ongoing supervision. This model advances public safety while reducing our reliance on incarceration. Programs like Common Justice cost significantly less than incarceration on Rikers Island and produce strong outcomes for both survivors and responsible parties. Instead of relying on a system that too often fails to address the root causes of violence, we invest in

community-based responses that help people access housing, employment and support in the neighborhoods where they live. For these reasons, we urge the Council to continue and expand investments in alternatives to incarceration and other community-based responses to violence. These programs hold people accountable, support survivors and strengthen public safety while reducing the city’s needs on– the city’s reliance on incarceration. Thank you for your time.
